sections.heading: The quarter
sections.text: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) generated about $18.63 billion under DFB’s cash-capex free-cash-flow calculation in its fiscal 2027 first quarter, ended September 30, 2026—down about 27% from a year earlier. DFB defines this measure as operating cash flow minus cash additions to property and equipment. The comparison uses reported figures before rounding for presentation.

sections.heading: Dividends and other cash uses
sections.text: Cash dividends paid were about $6.76 billion, or roughly 36% of that measure. This comparison does not account for every competing use of cash: the amount left after dividends is not necessarily available for discretionary spending.

sections.heading: Finance leases
sections.text: Finance-lease principal also sits outside this cash-capex measure. Microsoft separately reported $1.0 billion of financing cash outflows from finance leases. Deducting that principal would produce a different analytical measure; lease interest already included in operating cash flow should not be deducted again.

sections.heading: The next comparison
sections.text: The next quarter will provide another comparison. For now, these figures describe one period—not a forecast of future dividends. Keeping cash capital spending, lease principal and distributions separate makes the change easier to interpret.

briefs.limitations: Cash-capex free cash flow is DFB-defined operating cash flow less cash additions to property and equipment, not an issuer-reported FCF figure. The additional lease-principal deduction is analytical. Derived figures are arithmetic on rounded reported inputs; the dividend remainder excludes other investing and financing cash flows. One quarter does not establish future distribution capacity.

sections.heading: Cash generation
sections.text: Keurig Dr Pepper’s November 3 earnings release details cash generation alongside substantial financing obligations. For the first nine months of 2026, operating cash flow was $2.220 billion. Subtracting $457 million of property, plant and equipment purchases and adding $145 million of disposal proceeds produces KDP’s reported non-GAAP free cash flow of $1.908 billion.

sections.heading: Other financing claims
sections.text: Common cash dividends of $938 million leave a calculated $970 million difference against that free-cash-flow measure. This is before other financing uses, including $107 million of preferred dividends, $64 million of distributions to non-controlling interests and $146 million of finance-lease payments. Excluding property-disposal proceeds, operating cash flow less PP&E purchases was $1.763 billion; this is a separate calculation, not KDP’s defined free cash flow.

sections.heading: Current obligations
sections.text: At September 30, KDP reported $1.290 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $7.270 billion of short-term borrowings and the current portion of long-term obligations. That balance-sheet classification alone does not establish individual repayment dates.

sections.heading: What remains
sections.text: The near-term question is how much cash remains after distributions and other commitments as the company works toward its planned separation. The release supports a cash-coverage observation, not a dividend-safety guarantee.

briefs.limitations: Issuer-defined non-GAAP free cash flow includes PP&E disposal proceeds. The common-dividend difference is not unrestricted or discretionary cash and excludes other investing and financing uses. Operating cash flow less PP&E purchases is a separate analytical measure. Balance-sheet current classification alone is not an individual repayment schedule. Historical cash coverage is not a guarantee or forecast of dividends. The release financial statements are unaudited. Exhibit 99.1 is furnished under Item 2.02, not deemed filed for Section 18; issuer and SEC copies are two official representations of the same company statement, not independent economic corroboration.

sections.heading: Charge and cash
sections.text: 3M’s November 4 filing separates a $7.35 billion nominal settlement commitment from a planned pretax charge of approximately $5.8 billion. sections.heading: Payment timing

sections.heading: Conditional schedule

Actual amounts and timing depend on participation and other conditions; all payments after the initial one are contingent on neither party exercising termination rights.

sections.heading: What remains
sections.text: 3M says the charge will be treated as a special item in adjusted results and leaves its 2026 guidance unchanged. That accounting treatment does not remove future cash obligations. The question to follow is how settlement participation and conditions translate into actual payments alongside the company’s other commitments.

briefs.limitations: This record describes settlement terms as of November 3, 2026, not a historical operating reporting period. The filing was dated November 3 but the SEC index gives a November 4 filing date; no exact public-availability timestamp is claimed. No estimate of dividend coverage or dividend safety is made. sections.heading: Completed new issue
sections.text: Apple completed a $7.5 billion debt issue on November 9, selling seven series of senior unsecured notes. Of that principal, $3.25 billion matures in 2028 and 2029, about 43% of the new borrowing. The remaining maturities extend through 2036, according to its new SEC filing.

sections.heading: Rate structure
sections.text: The issue combines $6.25 billion of fixed-rate notes, with annual coupons ranging from 4.65% to 5.35%, and $1.25 billion of floating-rate notes. The floating rates reset quarterly using compounded SOFR plus contractual spreads. These are the terms of this issue, not Apple’s entire debt portfolio.

sections.heading: Two separate exposures
sections.text: The structure separates interest-rate exposure from repayment timing. Fixed coupons keep the stated interest rate unchanged, but the principal still comes due on schedule. Floating coupons leave interest payments exposed to changes in the reference rate. Neither feature establishes how Apple will fund the eventual repayments.

sections.heading: Actual use remains unspecified
sections.text: Apple’s prospectus estimated approximately $7.47 billion of net proceeds after underwriting discounts and expenses. It lists buybacks and dividends among several possible corporate uses, alongside investment and debt repayment. How much ultimately goes to each purpose remains unspecified; the borrowing alone does not demonstrate that dividends require debt funding.

limitations: November 9 is actual completed issuance and SEC filing date. November 5 is the underwriting agreement date and earliest event on the cover; it is not presented as the completion date. The prospectus was dated November 5 and filed November 6.
The reporting period is the point-in-time November 9 issuance, not an accounting quarter. The estimated net proceeds are a separately declared November 5 offering estimate.
All principal figures are face amounts of this new issue only, not net proceeds or total Apple debt. The $3.25 billion figure adds four series maturing November 9, 2028 and November 9, 2029.
The calculated 43 percent is 3250/7500*100 rounded to the nearest whole percent. Remaining principal matures in 2031, 2033 and 2036.

Fixed coupons are not yield to maturity or an assertion of Apple’s effective post-hedge financing costs. Floating rates reset quarterly based on compounded SOFR plus contractual spreads. No total interest-expense forecast is made.

The $7.47 billion net-proceeds figure is an approximate issuer estimate, not confirmed final realized proceeds. Permitted general corporate uses do not establish actual allocation or a need to borrow to pay dividends.

Both primary documents are issuer-authored SEC filings. No separate bond press release was found on Apple investor relations; the actual final prospectus supplement is the issuer supplement, accurately labeled as SEC-hosted. No recommendation, valuation conclusion or safety guarantee is made.

sections.text: TSMC’s board approved approximately US$40.93 billion in capital appropriations on November 10, alongside a NT$9-per-common-share dividend for the third quarter of 2026. The decisions put shareholder distributions and substantial investment plans on the same agenda.

sections.heading: Dividend and earnings
sections.text: The dividend equals about 31% of the quarter’s NT$29.43 diluted earnings per share, an earnings comparison rather than cash-flow coverage. Common shareholders have a March 11, 2027 ex-dividend date, a March 17 record date and an April 8 payment date. The NT$9 figure is not a per-ADS amount.

sections.heading: Capital scope
sections.text: The capital authorization covers manufacturing and packaging capacity, fab construction and facility systems, plus 2027 research-and-development investment, sustaining expenditures and capitalized leased assets. Appropriations authorize projects; they do not establish that US$40.93 billion has already been spent or that the entire amount belongs to one year’s cash-capex budget.

sections.heading: Investment timing
sections.text: Separately, directors approved up to US$500 million for Anthropic common shares at its initial-public-offering price and up to US$500 million for OpenAI preferred stock. These are investment ceilings, not disclosed completed purchases. The filing leaves the timing of these cash outlays, and their interaction with future operating cash generation, unresolved.

sections.heading: Special distribution
sections.text: Costco (NASDAQ: COST) declared a $30-per-share special cash dividend on November 10, 2026, with an estimated total payment of $13.3 billion. The dividend is payable on December 4, 2026, to common shareholders of record at the close of business on November 24. Its Form 8-K and accompanying release set out the terms.

sections.heading: Replacement authorization
sections.text: The board also reauthorized up to $4 billion of common-stock repurchases through November 2030. This replaces a $4 billion program adopted in 2023 that was scheduled to expire in January 2027. Costco said $3.1 billion had already been purchased under that earlier program.

sections.heading: Unused authorization comparison
sections.text: Subtracting reported purchases from the old ceiling leaves roughly $0.9 billion of unused authorization. On those rounded figures, the replacement increases available repurchase capacity by approximately $3.1 billion, rather than adding $4 billion to the unused balance. Authorization does not mean the purchases have occurred.

sections.heading: Spending and funding limits
sections.text: The release does not specify a funding plan for the special dividend or a timetable for using the repurchase authorization. It establishes a distribution date and a buyback ceiling, rather than a combined cash-spending forecast.

briefs.limitations: The estimated total special-dividend payment and reported repurchases are rounded issuer amounts. Unused authorization is calculated from the old ceiling and disclosed cumulative purchases as of the announcement, not a cash balance. The new program replaces the earlier authorization; neither authorization is a completed cash outflow. The release does not specify funding or an execution schedule, and this brief makes no coverage, yield or future dividend prediction.

sections.heading: Quarterly cash allocation
sections.text: Applied Materials (NASDAQ: AMAT) spent $2 billion on share repurchases and $421 million on dividends in its fiscal fourth quarter ended October 25, 2026. Those payments nearly matched the semiconductor-equipment maker’s $2.616 billion in non-GAAP free cash flow, according to results released on November 12 and furnished to the SEC.

sections.heading: Cash flow definition
sections.text: The company generated $3.3 billion in operating cash and spent $684 million on capital expenditures. Subtracting that spending produces its reported free-cash-flow measure. This is cash after capital investment, not net income, and it does not deduct shareholder distributions.

sections.heading: Arithmetic and boundary
sections.text: Buybacks and dividends together totaled $2.421 billion, leaving a calculated difference of $195 million against free cash flow. That difference is not an increase in cash on hand: the cash-flow statement separately includes investment transactions, share-issuance proceeds and $133 million of tax withholding on vested equity awards.

sections.heading: No recurring commitment
sections.text: The quarter shows how closely these shareholder payments tracked cash generated after capital spending. It does not establish that the same buyback pace will recur, or that this comparison captures every demand on the company’s cash.

briefs.limitations: The calculation compares reported quarterly operating cash less capital expenditures with common-stock repurchases and dividends. It is not a complete cash bridge: equity-award tax withholding, investment transactions, issuance proceeds and other movements are separate. It is not a recurring distribution forecast or a dividend-safety assessment.

sections.heading: Reported quarterly outlays
sections.text: Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) spent $3.651 billion on program share repurchases and dividends in its fiscal first quarter ended October 24, 2026. Its November 12 earnings release also disclosed a separate $414 million payment for shares repurchased to cover taxes when restricted stock units vested.

sections.heading: Cash comparison
sections.text: Operating cash flow of $4.357 billion less $502 million spent on property and equipment leaves $3.855 billion, calculated by DFB. Program buybacks and dividends were $204 million below that amount. Adding the separate equity-withholding outlay brings the combined payments to $4.065 billion, or $210 million above cash generated after this capital spending.

sections.heading: Different categories
sections.text: The distinction matters because the withholding payment is reported separately from the company’s stock-repurchase program. It should not be silently combined with program buybacks or treated as an additional dividend. The figures are quarterly cash movements, not earnings or future repurchase commitments.

sections.heading: Limits of comparison

briefs.limitations: Cash after property and equipment spending is a DFB calculation, not an unrestricted cash balance. Program buybacks, dividends and equity tax withholding are distinct outlays. sections.heading: The margin comparison
sections.text: TJX’s third-quarter pretax profit margin rose to 13.0% from 12.7% a year earlier, but the comparison changed after tariff refunds and related compensation expenses were excluded. The company reported an adjusted margin of 12.5%, below the prior-year level, in its November 18 earnings release.

sections.heading: Refunds and compensation
sections.text: For the quarter ended October 31, 2026, TJX received $132 million in refunds of previously paid International Emergency Economic Powers Act tariffs. It also accrued $55 million of incremental expenses for year-end incentive compensation and non-executive discretionary bonuses. Subtracting those expenses produces the $77 million net pretax benefit reported by the company.

sections.heading: Different measures
sections.text: That distinction matters when reading the margin trend. The reported measure improved by 0.3 percentage points, while the company’s adjusted measure declined by 0.2 points. The adjustment removes both the refund benefit and the related compensation expense accruals, rather than treating every dollar received as an addition to pretax profit.

sections.heading: Limits of the comparison
sections.text: The refund receipts and compensation accruals also describe different accounting events: an expense accrual does not establish when cash will be paid. Whether subsequent quarters show a similar margin pattern remains open. This quarter’s reconciliation does not establish recurring earnings or cash available for distributions.

briefs.limitations: Company-defined adjusted margin is not GAAP margin. Refund receipts are not equivalent to net pretax income; compensation accruals are not asserted to be current cash payments. One quarter does not establish recurring earnings or distribution capacity.

sections.heading: Cash and capital spending
sections.text: Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) generated more operating cash in the nine months ended October 31, 2026, yet its free cash flow fell. The company’s November 19 release reported $29.436 billion of operating cash and $22.621 billion of payments for property and equipment, leaving $6.815 billion under its free-cash-flow definition.

sections.heading: The year-over-year bridge
sections.text: A year earlier, operating cash was $27.452 billion and property-and-equipment payments were $18.627 billion, producing $8.825 billion of free cash flow. The arithmetic explains the reversal: operating cash increased by $1.984 billion, but capital spending rose by $3.994 billion. Free cash flow therefore declined by $2.010 billion.

sections.heading: Other uses and timing
sections.text: Walmart attributed the capital-spending increase to its omnichannel growth strategy. Operating cash also reflected payment timing and inventory receipts, so its improvement should not be read solely as a change in underlying profitability. The cash-flow statement separately shows $5.913 billion of dividends and $7.830 billion of company-stock purchases.

sections.heading: What the measure leaves out
sections.text: These are nine-month totals, not third-quarter cash flows alone. Walmart’s non-GAAP free cash flow is not residual cash available for discretionary spending: its definition does not deduct debt service, other contractual obligations or acquisition payments. Whether operating cash can keep pace with investment remains a question for subsequent periods, not a conclusion from this release.

briefs.limitations: Nine-month totals, not Q3 alone. Company-defined non-GAAP free cash flow is operating cash less payments for property and equipment, not residual discretionary cash. Timing influences operating cash and no future distribution capacity is established.

sections.heading: Cash returned
sections.text: Analog Devices (NASDAQ: ADI) returned about $5.41 billion in cash dividends and share repurchases in its fiscal year ended October 31, 2026. That was approximately 99% of its $5.45 billion in free cash flow, based on the cash-flow statement furnished with the chipmaker’s November 24 Form 8-K.

sections.heading: Full-year comparison
sections.text: Analog Devices defines its non-GAAP free cash flow as operating cash flow less net additions to property, plant and equipment. On that basis, free cash flow rose about 27% from fiscal 2025. But repurchases increased faster than cash dividends and accounted for most of the increase in cash returned to shareholders. The combined figure includes repurchases already made, not unused buyback authorization.

sections.heading: Other uses of cash
sections.text: That comparison leaves out other investing and financing flows. The company separately reported about $1.54 billion in acquisition payments, net of cash acquired. The 99% figure therefore describes how shareholder payouts compared with free cash flow over the year. It does not show that a particular payout was funded with debt. Whether buybacks continue at that pace remains an open question.

limitations: Free cash flow is a non-GAAP measure and excludes acquisition payments and financing flows. The comparison does not attribute specific financing proceeds to a payment.
